technique: the second person — how 'you' pulls the reader into the room
lesson:
Today we work on one tool: the second person. That means the poem says "you" and "your," so the reader stands in the spot the poem describes.

Look where it does this. "your bare hand / takes it anyway." "You stand there a breath, hand flat to the metal." "letting the cold tell you plainly where you are." Each time, the word "you" puts the listener's own hand on that cold door.

It works because your brain treats "you" as a direct address. You hear "your hand" and you supply your own hand. You stop watching someone else and start doing the thing yourself. That pulls you into the cold and the morning.

Try this: write one line about an ordinary action, then rewrite it with "you" and "your" so the reader does it.

The second time through, count every "you" and "your" and feel your attention get tugged in each time.

Here is the poem.
poem:
Cold iron of the truck door, and your bare hand
takes it anyway, that first bright shock that says
the night went down past freezing one more time—
the eighth such morning this dry month, the grass
gone stiff and silver, no rain to speak of yet,
the ground still not quite locked, just thinking on it.
A month of frost and a month still till the sun
turns back around and starts the long climb home.
You stand there a breath, hand flat to the metal,
letting the cold tell you plainly where you are:
awake, and wanted, with a day that leans toward noon
and someone's name in it, warm as the stove banked low.

Cold morning, warm bed, but the fire you build is better than the one you'd miss—
go strike it.
